records.name: Armenia
records.summary:
Armenia demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Armenia has no anti-LGBT legislation of the Georgian or Russian type — and an administrative practice for legal gender recognition exists (medicalised). Pink Armenia's 2024 annual report documents ongoing violations including inhuman/degrading treatment, and hate speech is routine in public discourse; the 2018 failed anti-discrimination bill means there is still no SOGI-specific protection statute. Yerevan has a small organised community (Pink Armenia, Right Side — a trans-led NGO), but visibility carries real risk.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; social hostility significant outside central Yerevan; police response unreliable.

sources.claim: Pink Human Rights Defender NGO annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024. Documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech - including a chapter on pressure around a transgender individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Equaldex comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia: Armenia decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections 'ambiguous' since 2022; no SOGI discrimination protections; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low (5/100).

ILGA-Europe/COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in Armenia.

Unzipped: Gay Armenia blog (May 2012): neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan - Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via CCTV - documents anti-LGBT hate violence in Armenia.

The Guardian (April 2019): Armenia's first registered trans woman, Lilit Martirosyan, received death threats (including MPs calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination - documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.

records.name: American Samoa
records.summary:
No criminal exposure: the territory's own legislature decriminalised same-sex conduct in the 1979 code revision (effective 1980), age of consent equal at 16. No local protections of practical substance exist: nothing criminalises a trans visitor, and next to nothing shields one.

Partner travel is the sharpest edge. Marriages performed elsewhere must be recognised under a 2022 federal statute, yet the territory performs none: officials long treated the 2015 federal ruling as 'under review', a judge said in 2016 he would not apply it, and licences remain withheld through 2024-26 — a 2026 review concludes any same-sex applicant must be served, but none has applied, so on-island spousal recognition is untested.

Social climate is conservative and church-centred, reserved behaviour expected; yet it is the homeland of a widely accepted indigenous third-gender presence; trans-presenting travellers more often meet cultural familiarity than the hostility recorded in some neighbouring islands. Net: low state risk, thin institutional cover, reliance on informal tolerance.

sources.claim: UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities (maintained; last updated 2026-07-23). Contains substantive American Samoa content: the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride - 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.claim: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. For this record: documents that the territory deliberately declined a formal marriage ban pre-Obergefell, and gives contemporaneous local fa'afafine voices on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.claim: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. For this record: direct evidence that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise it did not automatically apply, with named actors and dates.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.claim: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. For this record: the freshest dated authority on the exact open question (is the 2015 ruling operative in ASM?), and it separates the law from the practical reality (no licenses sought/issued).

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.claim: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). For this record: as of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

freshness.question: (a) Does Obergefell apply in ASM today; what happened since 2015 'still reviewing'?
freshness.fact: ASM performs no same-sex marriages. The 2022 federal Respect for Marriage Act forces recognition of unions performed elsewhere.

freshness.fact: First sodomy law 1963; Fono removed it in the 1979 criminal-code revision, effective 1980. Age of consent equal at 16 regardless of gender/orientation.

freshness.fact: Birth-certificate edits limited to record errors; gender marker may change only with medical documentation; no local discrimination protections.

freshness.fact: No new law/ruling/incident located; 2026 law-review article (ASM Legal Aid/FFRF) argues Obergefell must apply; marriage licences still withheld on-island.

records.name: Antigua and Barbuda
records.summary: Antigua and Barbuda demands real caution. The High Court struck down the buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Jul 2022): 'Antigua and Barbuda: High Court Decriminalizes Gay Sex' — the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court strikes down the 'sodomy' and 'gross indecency' provisions.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): in 2022 the High Court found Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional, decriminalising same-sex conduct, and interpreted 'sex' discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity. However, no explicit antidiscrimination protections exist, same-sex unions are not recognised, and trans people are particularly vulnerable because there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers - only name changes.

El País/AP (June 2023): profile of Orden David, the Antiguan LGBTQ activist who challenged the country's anti-sodomy law and won in 2022 - he had been bullied and physically attacked (struck in the head, knocked out in daylight); the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruled the law unconstitutional; six Caribbean countries still criminalise.

St Lucia Star (Dec 2019): ECADE announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing the laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence.

The Advocates for Human Rights (January 2025): submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for Antigua and Barbuda listing LGBTQ+ rights issues ahead of its review — documents the open SOGI-protection questions the state still faces post-2022 decriminalisation.

records.name: Australia
records.summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court's landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Aug 2024) covers a trans woman winning a landmark discrimination case against a female-only dating app in Australia.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying Queensland Human Rights Commission item concerned strengthened discrimination protections for gender-diverse people under Queensland's anti-discrimination law reform.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 400); this was a NSW Parliament bill document (PDF), not retrievable at fetch time.

ANROWS research briefing: maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia — organised exclusionary campaigns, facilities and records-access disputes, rights-rollback pressures: the live opposition landscape a trans visitor moves through despite strong statutes.

Queensland Parliamentary Library research brief (2003) 'Protecting Transgender Rights under Queensland's Discrimination Law Amendment Act 2002': introduced 'gender identity' as a protected attribute; documents trans people's difficulties with sex designations on passports, licences and birth certificates, high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places.

Organisation Intersex International Australia briefing: argues intersex is not a gender identity and warns against folding intersex into SOGI legal frameworks (recommends SOGIESC terminology) — relevant to how Australian gender-diversity protections are scoped.

Australian Lesbian & Gay Archives, 'Towards Homosexual Equality in Australian Criminal Law - A Brief History' (Carbery, 2nd ed. 2014): state-by-state history of decriminalisation, from British-inherited buggery laws (death penalty in Victoria until 1949) through reform - historical legal context for Australia's current framework.

freshness.fact: Marriage equality (2017); federal hate-crime offence Feb 2025; conversion-therapy bans ~85% of pop. since Oct 2024 — far beyond pre-2017 state.

records.name: Austria
records.summary:
Austria is a workable destination with a notably more conservative climate and a live far-right government hostility signal. The governing Freedom Party (FPÖ) mocks gender-diverse people publicly and has pledged a constitutional "two sexes" definition that would repeal non-binary protections — a threat, not yet enacted.

The most concrete traveler-relevant risk is organised dating-app predation: in 2025 authorities uncovered a neo-Nazi network that lured, beat, humiliated and filmed victims — primarily gay and bisexual men — through fake dating profiles (15 arrested). Caution is warranted on dating apps for queer travelers. There is no bathroom restriction law, no cross-dressing statute, and no documented border-police humiliation of trans travelers.

If detained, there are no specific legal protections for trans detainees — they are housed with the general population on an ad-hoc basis (only three trans people were in detention as of mid-2025). Trans-specific hate incidents actually declined in 2025, though homophobic violence rose.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Austria. Documents a neo-Nazi network uncovered in March that used fake dating profiles to lure gay and bisexual men to ambushes by masked assailants (attacks filmed and shared); a rejected Vienna petition for queer sauna time slots; new Ministry of Education rules restricting outside sex-education providers; and Ombud guidance for gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people.

Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Austria, part of an EU-funded project. Covers the legal framework for LGBTIQ people in detention, gender self-determination, anti-discrimination protection, and the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons.

Austrian Justice Ministry answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 (May-June 2025): official rules on housing transgender people in Austrian penal institutions — the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained; German-language.

DW report (March 2025): Austrian police arrested 15 people (aged 14-26) over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed, and falsely accused of being paedophiles. Investigators believe the real victim count is much higher.

The Local Austria (July 2026): Austria recorded 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives in 2025, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence; police data broken down by who faces violent hate crime, while acknowledging under-recording.

GGG (July 2026): official Austrian hate-crime statistics for the reporting year show homophobic offences rising while transphobic incidents declined — against 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence in 2025 (The Local, same data).

PinkNews (Sept 2024): Austria's far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) won the most votes in a national election for the first time since WWII (29.2%), raising concerns about what an FPÖ-led government could mean for LGBTQ+ people.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity legal since 1971, marriage equality since 2017, full adoption rights since 2016. Legal gender recognition is possible without mandatory medical procedures, and individuals may obtain an 'X', indeterminate, or no gender marker; intersex people can choose 'diverse', 'inter', or no designation. Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation, with recent amendments broadening 'gender' to include gender identity, expression and sex characteristics.

PinkNews (May 2019): Austria recognised a third gender option in official documents - intersex activist Alex Jürgen received the country's first non-binary passport ('X' marker) and birth certificate ('divers'), following the June 2018 Constitutional Court ruling that gender identity must be accurately reflected in official documents; the Interior Ministry restricted 'divers' to people with a medical panel certificate of intersexuality.

freshness.fact: Legal framework unchanged: third-gender registration option (since 2019) stands; no 2024-26 amendments or rollbacks in current sources.

records.name: Azerbaijan
records.summary:
Azerbaijan is dangerous for trans visitors. The documented pattern is grim: a trans woman was tortured and murdered in Baku in July 2023; a second trans woman's murder in March 2024 was met with a police response lacking comprehensive investigation; several other trans people were physically assaulted, including by police themselves; and two trans women were detained for “hooliganism” for making noise. Government-affiliated media air targeted discriminatory hate speech. Trans people face total economic marginalisation (black-market work, precarious housing).

Nothing formally criminalises gender expression, but police are perpetrators rather than protectors, and the state is one of the world's more closed authoritarian systems — there is no recourse and no community infrastructure that can operate openly. An April 2024 ECtHR ruling found violations in Azerbaijan's treatment of LGBTI applicants.

For a visitor: no statute bars entry or expression, but discovery risks police abuse with no remedy, and the murder-impunity pattern is documented.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents the March murder of a trans woman in Baku met with an inadequate police investigation; state-affiliated Real TV airing discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding trans healthcare access; a family forcibly transporting an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out; and an April ECtHR ruling on the September 2017 police arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, which Azerbaijan acknowledged in 2019.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents a July police raid on a private birthday party where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of outing; QueeRadar monitoring found 77% of 428 analysed media pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people; and an activist being told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe.

OC Media feature by Ali Malikov on trans people in Azerbaijan: discrimination has direct economic impacts - trans people are rejected from jobs and housing, pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. Profiles 'Durdana', 29, arrested, denied housing and employment, and dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

HRW (Oct 2017): Azerbaijan's anti-gay crackdown — police raids in Baku (Sept 2017) detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges with beatings documented; HRW called for investigation and release.

Gender & Development Social Union shadow report to CEDAW (44th session) on discrimination and violence against lesbian, bisexual and transgender people in Azerbaijan: documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia/transphobia in official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women; the organisation serves 200+ LBT people.

The Guardian (Sept 2017): outcry as Azerbaijan police launch crackdown on the LGBT community - at least 60 people imprisoned or fined after raids in the capital; part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games.

freshness.fact: No protections, hostile enforcement: mass Baku arrest waves with beatings/forced exams; strong stigma; the ILGA-2025 review picture remains current.

records.name: Burundi
records.summary: Burundi is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Same-sex conduct has been criminalised since 2009 (2 years), and the head of state himself has called for mob violence: in December 2023, President Ndayishimiye said LGBT people should be “taken to a stadium and stoned” because “that's what they deserve” — condemned by HRW as stoking fear; the Iteka League called it a call to lynching. There is no LGR, no community infrastructure (the oldest rights group works from exile), and arbitrary detention is routine.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Jan 2024): 'Burundi President Stokes Fear Among LGBT People' — President Ndayishimiye's call to 'stone' homosexuals; HRW urges the ruling party to renounce persecution.

SOS Médias Burundi (Jan 2024): after President Évariste Ndayishimiye called for 'homosexuals to be stoned', LGBTQ Burundians reported terror; the Iteka League (in exile) called the remarks 'a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people'. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the remarks as 'a real license to kill (us)'. Same-sex relations are criminalised in Burundi.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents the country's crisis (extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, media shutdowns) and includes the section on acts of violence and discrimination against LGBT persons - same-sex conduct criminalised since 2009, with arrests and harassment documented.
US State Department 2009 Human Rights Report for Burundi (archived): covers the year the penal code criminalised same-sex conduct; documents discrimination against gays and lesbians.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Burundi: lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among common human-rights abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents torture, extrajudicial executions, prolonged pretrial detention, and discrimination against LGBT persons under the criminalised framework.

freshness.fact: Same-sex acts still criminalised; Ndayishimiye's Dec-2023 'choosing Satan'/death-penalty rhetoric keeps a climate of fear.

records.name: Belgium
records.summary:
Belgium is a top-tier destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender and name change by self-declaration has been available since 2018, anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and expression across employment, housing and services, hate crime and hate speech are both criminalised for gender identity, and transphobia is a separately tracked hate-crime motive. Belgium also passed Europe's first femicide law (2023), with protections for gender minorities.

The framework is politically stable with no rollback movement — a contrast with several neighbours (the UK's in-force facilities code, Portugal's first-reading repeal attempt, Germany's repeal review). The main caveat is a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ violence and intimidation: the equality body Unia reported in 2025 that gay men and transgender people are increasingly targeted, and an RTBF investigation documented dating-app ambush attacks on queer men in urban nightlife.

For a visitor this is a comfortable environment with the usual urban-nightlife caution: zero legal exposure, functioning institutions, and a welcoming day-to-day climate, particularly in Brussels.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Belgium has robust protections - discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of SOGISC banned; same-sex marriage and adoption; legal name and gender-marker change based on self-determination. Europe's first femicide law (2023) covers all gender-based homicide; a 2023 law bans conversion practices. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, though a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for nonconsensual interventions.

ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Belgium: overall index score plus per-category compliance (legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality & non-discrimination, family, civil society, asylum, intersex) — the formal-law snapshot of Belgium's framework.

VRT NWS (May 2025): despite Belgium's progressive reputation, equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men report rising violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by Unia in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is 'dating app traps' - gay men lured via apps, ambushed, beaten and robbed; a high-profile case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

KET Magazine (Feb 2025) summarising an RTBF investigation into rising homophobic attacks in Belgium orchestrated through dating apps: perpetrators use fake profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations where they are robbed, humiliated or assaulted. Police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported due to fear or shame.

OSCE/ODIHR page on Belgium's national hate-crime frameworks: hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation and no code exists to record them as such; violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions instead.

Official Brussels-Capital Region page on changing gender registration on ID cards: free of charge, 3-6 weeks processing, requires a valid identity document, a medical certificate attesting to sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision; application made in person at the commune, digital mode available.

Belgian Federal Justice Department page: since 1 January 2018 (Law of 25 June 2017), trans people can change registered gender and first names without medical conditions, via a declaration to the civil registrar. On 19 June 2019 the Constitutional Court partially annulled the law; pending new provisions, applications continue under the current procedure.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Belgium is 'one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers in the world', with forward-thinking attitudes and thriving queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège.

Discovering Belgium guide (2024): overview of LGBT+ rights history and current status - sex between men decriminalised as far back as 1795 under the French penal code, though public-indecency laws and police harassment persisted; covers key figures, organisations, current rights, and where to report homophobia.

'Being transgender in Belgium - Ten years later' (2017), by Motmans, Wyverkens, Defreyne et al. for the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men: a large survey study of trans people in Belgium covering gender identity, coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed per experienced gender, official name/gender registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

Press release (May 2017, in Dutch) from Justice Minister Koen Geens on Belgium's new transgender law: self-determination is the starting point - legal gender change via a purely administrative procedure with all medical conditions (including sterilisation/surgery) scrapped; includes a reflection period and public-order safeguards; notes name-change requests rose from 85 (2012) to 187 (2016).

freshness.fact: Progressive frame intact: self-declaration gender-recognition law, conversion practices banned Jul 2023, equal marriage/adoption; no 2024-26 regression.
